## Short-range dependent stochastic processes

The random-walk model introduced in the previous post is not the only experimentally relevant stochastic process. In fact, it is often an extreme case. A random walk possesses infinite memory: once a perturbation affects the system, its effect is never progressively forgotten. The variance therefore grows indefinitely with time, and the process continuously accumulates uncertainty.

Many real physical systems behave differently. Mechanical damping, thermal relaxation, fluid dynamics, electronic feedback, and dissipative phenomena of various kinds often produce stochastic dynamics that gradually lose memory of their past. In these situations, random perturbations still affect the state evolution, but their influence progressively fades away over time.

One of the simplest and most important stochastic models capturing this behavior is the first-order Gauss--Markov (GM1) process.

In continuous time, the scalar GM1 model can be written as

$$
\dot x(t)=-b\,x(t)+w(t),
$$

where $b>0$ controls the correlation time of the process and $w(t)$ is continuous-time white Gaussian noise with strength $q$:

$$
R_{WW}(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[w(t)w(t+\tau)]=q\,\delta(\tau).
$$

The term $-b\,x(t)$ continuously pulls the process back toward equilibrium, while the stochastic excitation injects random fluctuations into the dynamics.

Unlike a random walk, the GM1 process is stationary: after an initial transient, its variance converges to a finite asymptotic value instead of diverging indefinitely.

The corresponding autocorrelation function is

$$
R_{XX}(\tau)=\sigma_X^2 e^{-b|\tau|},
$$

showing that the process progressively forgets its past over the characteristic correlation time

$$
\tau_c = \frac{1}{b}.
$$ {#eq-2}

This model is far from a purely theoretical construction. Closely related stochastic dynamics naturally emerge in many experimental settings, including inertial sensing, ultrasonic time-of-flight measurements, oscillator stability analysis, and barometric pressure sensing, where temporally correlated fluctuations often become a dominant source of uncertainty.

An important feature of the GM1 process for Kalman filtering is that its continuous-time dynamics admit an exact discrete-time representation.

If measurements are acquired every $\Delta T$ seconds, the corresponding discrete-time model becomes

$$
x_{k+1}=F\,x_k+\Delta w_k,
$$ {#eq-1}

with

$$
F=e^{-b\Delta T},
$$

where $\Delta w_k$ represents the stochastic increment resulting from integrating white noise over the sampling interval $\Delta T$.

The corresponding discrete-time process-noise variance is

$$
Q=\sigma_X^2\left(1-e^{-2b\,\Delta T}\right),
$$

or equivalently,

$$
Q=\frac{q}{2b}\left(1-e^{-2b\,\Delta T}\right).
$$

Unlike the random-walk case, the process noise injected between consecutive samples now depends not only on the sampling interval, but also on the finite correlation time of the underlying dynamics.

This exact discretization is particularly important because it preserves the statistical structure of the continuous-time process independently of the chosen sampling interval.

Several limiting situations immediately emerge from these expressions. For very small sampling intervals, $F\approx 1-b\,\Delta T$ and $Q\approx q\,\Delta T$, and the process locally behaves like the random walk introduced in the previous post. Conversely, for sampling intervals much longer than the correlation time, (F\to 0) and (Q\to\sigma\_X\^2), meaning that consecutive samples progressively lose statistical dependence and the process approaches a memoryless regime.

For stationary scalar systems, the steady-state updated covariance satisfies the algebraic Riccati equation

$$
P_\infty=F^2P_\infty+Q-\frac{(F^2P_\infty+Q)^2}{F^2P_\infty+Q+R}.
$$ {#eq-3}

The corresponding steady-state Kalman gain is therefore

$$
K_\infty=\frac{F^2P_\infty+Q}{F^2P_\infty+Q+R}.
$$ {#eq-4}

where the positive steady-state solution is

$$
P_\infty=\frac{-\left(Q+R-RF^2\right)+\sqrt{\left(Q+R-RF^2\right)^2+4F^2RQ}}{2F^2}.
$$ {#eq-5}

After the initial transient, the filter behaves as a stationary recursive estimator with constant asymptotic gain.

## The AR(1) perspective

The exact discrete-time representation of the sampled GM1 process is mathematically equivalent to the first-order autoregressive process, usually denoted AR(1):

$$
x_{k+1}=\phi\,x_k+\eta_k,
$$

where $\phi\equiv F$ and $\eta_k\equiv \Delta w_k$ represent respectively the transition coefficient and the discrete-time stochastic increment introduced earlier (@eq-1), with:

$$
\phi=e^{-\Delta T/\tau_c},
$$

where $\tau_c$ is the correlation time of the underlying continuous-time process (@eq-2).

This equivalence is important because it connects the continuous-time physical interpretation of the GM1 process with the classical theory of correlated discrete-time stochastic sequences.

For the sampled AR(1) process, the discrete-time autocorrelation sequence becomes

$$
r_{XX}[h]=\phi^{|h|},
$$

showing that adjacent samples become strongly correlated whenever $\phi$ approaches unity. This is precisely the situation encountered when the sampling interval $\Delta T$ is much shorter than the dominant correlation time of the physical process. Under these conditions, averaging no longer behaves as if the observations were independent.

For a sequence of $n$ correlated observations, the variance of the sample mean becomes

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_n)=\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n}\left[1+2\sum_{h=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{h}{n}\right)\phi^{h}\right].
$$

When $\phi=0$, corresponding to statistically independent observations, the classical result is immediately recovered:

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_n)=\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n}.
$$

However, when $\phi$ is close to unity, consecutive samples carry strongly redundant information and the reduction of uncertainty through averaging becomes much slower than the familiar $1/\sqrt{n}$ law associated with white noise.

In practical terms, this means that increasing the sampling frequency within the dominant correlation-time range of the process may provide far less statistical benefit than expected under independence assumptions.

## Simulation

The exact discrete-time GM1 model can now be inserted directly into the scalar Kalman filter. In this simulation, the filter is deliberately matched to the process that generated the data: the same values of $F$, $Q$, $H$, and $R$ are used both in the simulation model and in the estimator.

This is the cleanest situation to analyze first. Any discrepancy between the true state and the estimate is therefore not caused by model mismatch, but only by the unavoidable uncertainty induced by process and measurement noise.



::: {.cell}

```{.matlab .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Kalman filter perfectly matched to the Gauss-Markov process"}
% ********************************
% First-order Gauss-Markov process
% ********************************

b     = 0.5; % inverse of the correlation time, s^-1 
std_x = 1;   % stationary process standard deviation, [a.u.]
dt    = 1;   % sampling time, s
T     = 100; % observation time, s
std_v = 1;   % measurement error standard deviation, [a.u.]

% ***************
% Path generation
% ***************

rng(1250)

Ti  = 2*T;
dti = dt;

Ni = Ti/dti + 1;
N  = T/dt + 1;

xi = zeros(Ni, 1);

F_sim = exp(-b*dti);
Q_sim = std_x^2*(1 - exp(-2*b*dti));

for i = 2:Ni
    xi(i) = F_sim*xi(i-1) + randn*sqrt(Q_sim);
end

% Remove the first half to reduce dependence on initialization
x_true = xi((Ni-1)/2+1:dt/dti:end);

z_meas = x_true + randn(N, 1)*std_v;

% *******************
% Discrete-time model
% *******************

F = exp(-b*dt);
Q = std_x^2*(1 - exp(-2*b*dt));

H = 1;
R = std_v^2;

% **************
% Initialization
% **************

x_hat = zeros(N, 1);
P     = zeros(N, 1);
K     = zeros(N, 1);

x_pred = 0;
P_pred = std_x^2;

for i = 1:N

    % Kalman gain
    K(i) = P_pred*H/(H*P_pred*H + R);

    % Measurement update
    x_hat(i) = x_pred + K(i)*(z_meas(i) - H*x_pred);
    P(i) = (1 - K(i)*H)*P_pred;

    % Prediction
    x_pred = F*x_hat(i);
    P_pred = F*P(i)*F + Q;

end

% ************
% Error plot
% ************

figure
plot(0:N-1, x_hat - x_true, 'b', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(0:N-1,  2*sqrt(P), 'k--', ...
     0:N-1, -2*sqrt(P), 'k--', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
xlabel('Steps')
ylabel('Error state [a.u.]')
set(gca, 'FontSize', 14, 'LineWidth', 2)

% ****************
% Kalman gain plot
% ****************

figure
plot(0:N-1, K, 'b', 'LineWidth', 2)
xlabel('Steps')
ylabel('Kalman gain')
ylim([0 0.55])
set(gca, 'FontSize', 14, 'LineWidth', 2)
```
:::



@fig-error-state shows the estimation error together with the approximate 95% confidence bounds predicted by the filter. After the initial transient, the error behaves as expected for a correctly specified model: it fluctuates around zero and mostly remains within the predicted uncertainty bounds.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Estimation error and approximate 95% confidence bounds predicted by the KF ($\pm 2\sqrt{P_k}$). After the initial transient, the error remains mostly confined within the uncertainty interval associated with the estimated covariance.](error_state.png){#fig-error-state fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::



@fig-kf-gain shows the corresponding Kalman gain. After a short transient, the gain reaches a steady-state value, reflecting the stationary nature of the underlying process and the constant balance between prediction uncertainty and measurement uncertainty.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Evolution of the Kalman gain.](kf_gain.png){#fig-kf-gain fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::



For the parameters used in this simulation ($b=0.5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $\Delta t=1\,\mathrm{s}$, $\sigma_X=1\,\mathrm{a.u.}$, and $R=1\,(\mathrm{a.u.})^2$), the scalar Riccati equation (@eq-3) predicts a steady-state covariance (@eq-5) and Kalman gain (@eq-4) with the same numerical value, although the associated physical units differ:

$$
P_\infty=K_\infty \approx 0.443.
$$

This result is in excellent agreement with the simulated gain trajectory shown in @fig-kf-gain. The equality $P_\infty=K_\infty$ follows here from the scalar structure of the problem with $H=1$ and $R=1$.

## Probing the environment

The GM1 process introduced above should not be regarded merely as a convenient mathematical model. In many sensing problems, temporally correlated fluctuations are not merely a nuisance: they are the signature of the physical medium being observed.

A barometric pressure sensor, for example, does not only measure the electronic noise of its own readout chain. It also responds to slow pressure fluctuations, thermal effects, air motion, and environmental dynamics. Similarly, an ultrasonic time-of-flight system not only measures timing jitter: it probes the propagation medium, whose temperature, humidity, turbulence, and local gradients affect the measured delay.

In this sense, many sensors act as environmental probes. Their output contains information about the medium, but that information is rarely memoryless. The medium itself evolves continuously, and its fluctuations often possess a finite correlation time.

This is precisely the type of situation for which a GM1 model is useful. It provides a minimal description of a fluctuating physical quantity that is continuously perturbed, but also gradually forgets its past. The key point is that correlated noise is not always "bad noise". Sometimes it is the phenomenon of interest. What matters is not to average it away blindly, but to model its temporal structure correctly. The practical question then becomes: how much independent information is actually gained by sampling faster?

To answer this, we need a tool capable of showing how variability changes with averaging time.

## Allan deviation as a multiscale diagnostic tool

Allan deviation provides exactly this kind of multiscale view. Originally introduced in the context of oscillator stability analysis, it is now widely used for characterizing temporally correlated stochastic processes across many areas of measurement science and signal processing.

The following simulation reproduces a long-duration acquisition from a stationary GM1 process with correlation time

$$
\tau_c = 1\,\mathrm{s}.
$$

The process is sampled every

$$
T_s = 20\,\mathrm{ms},
$$

corresponding to an oversampling ratio of 50 samples per correlation time. The total observation time is approximately three hours (about 175 minutes), yielding a record of $2^{19}$ samples.

A white Gaussian sequence with the same stationary variance is generated as a reference for comparison. This allows the Allan-deviation analysis to isolate the effects of temporal correlation from those simply associated with signal amplitude.



::: {.cell}

```{.matlab .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Simulation of a long-term recording for Allan deviation analysis"}
% ***************************************
% GM1 signal for Allan deviation analysis
% ***************************************

clear
clc
close all

rng(2026)

% Physical / stochastic parameters

tau     = 1;      % correlation time [s]
std_y   = 1;      % stationary standard deviation [a.u.]
osr     = 50;     % samples per correlation time
Ts      = tau/osr;
Fs      = 1/Ts;

N       = 2^19;   % number of samples
t       = (0:N-1)'*Ts;

% Exact discrete-time GM1 model

F = exp(-Ts/tau);
Q = std_y^2*(1 - F^2);

y = zeros(N,1);

% Start at stationarity
y(1) = std_y*randn;

for k = 2:N
    y(k) = F*y(k-1) + sqrt(Q)*randn;
end

% White input sequence with same stationary variance for comparison

u = std_y*randn(N,1);

% Basic checks

fprintf('Sampling interval Ts = %.4g s\n', Ts)
fprintf('Observation time     = %.2f h\n', N*Ts/3600)
fprintf('Correlation time tau = %.4g s\n', tau)
fprintf('Empirical var white  = %.4g (a.u.)^2\n', var(u))
fprintf('Empirical var GM1    = %.4g (a.u.)^2\n', var(y))

% Save for Allan analyzer

save('allan_signals_gm1.mat', 'u', 'y', 't', 'Ts', 'Fs', 'tau', 'std_y', 'F', 'Q')

% Quick visualization

figure
plot(t(1:5000), u(1:5000), 'Color', [0.6 0.6 0.6])
hold on
plot(t(1:5000), y(1:5000), 'b', 'LineWidth', 1.2)
xlabel('Time [s]')
ylabel('Amplitude [a.u.]')
legend('white input', 'GM1 output')
set(gca, 'FontSize', 14, 'LineWidth', 1.5)
```
:::



The GM1 process can be interpreted as the output of a first-order stochastic shaping filter driven by white Gaussian noise. The following visualization compares the reference white-noise sequence with the corresponding correlated GM1 output generated by the discrete-time model. @fig-signal shows a short segment extracted from the simulated long-duration acquisition. Although the white-noise input and the GM1 output possess approximately the same variance, their temporal structure is profoundly different. The GM1 process appears visibly smoother because its dynamics suppress rapid fluctuations and introduce finite temporal correlation.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Short segment of the simulated white-noise input and corresponding GM1 output.](signals.png){#fig-signal fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.matlab .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Allan deviation analysis"}
% ************************
% Allan deviation analysis
% ************************

clear
clc
close all

load('allan_signals_gm1.mat')

% Cluster sizes: powers of two
N = length(u);
maxM = floor(N/8);
m = 2.^(0:floor(log2(maxM)));

% Allan variance
[avar_u, tau_u] = allanvar(u, m, Fs);
[avar_y, tau_y] = allanvar(y, m, Fs);

adev_u = sqrt(avar_u);
adev_y = sqrt(avar_y);

% Approximate number of Allan clusters
M = floor(N ./ m) - 1;

% Fit regions
idx_white     = tau_u >= 0.02 & tau_u <= 0.5;
idx_gm1_short = tau_y >= 0.02 & tau_y <= 0.5;
idx_gm1_long  = tau_y >= 20   & tau_y <= 500;

% Log-log weighted linear regression helper
fit_loglog = @(tau, adev, idx, M) fitlm( ...
    log10(tau(idx)), ...
    log10(adev(idx)), ...
    'linear', ...
    'Weights', M(idx));

mdl_white     = fit_loglog(tau_u, adev_u, idx_white, M);
mdl_gm1_short = fit_loglog(tau_y, adev_y, idx_gm1_short, M);
mdl_gm1_long  = fit_loglog(tau_y, adev_y, idx_gm1_long, M);

% Extract slopes and confidence intervals
ci_white     = coefCI(mdl_white);
ci_gm1_short = coefCI(mdl_gm1_short);
ci_gm1_long  = coefCI(mdl_gm1_long);

fprintf('White input slope    = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n', ...
    mdl_white.Coefficients.Estimate(2), ci_white(2,1), ci_white(2,2))

fprintf('GM1 short-time slope = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n', ...
    mdl_gm1_short.Coefficients.Estimate(2), ci_gm1_short(2,1), ci_gm1_short(2,2))

fprintf('GM1 long-time slope  = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n', ...
    mdl_gm1_long.Coefficients.Estimate(2), ci_gm1_long(2,1), ci_gm1_long(2,2))

% Fitted lines
tau_fit_white = tau_u(idx_white);
fit_white = 10.^predict(mdl_white, log10(tau_fit_white));

tau_fit_gm1_short = tau_y(idx_gm1_short);
fit_gm1_short = 10.^predict(mdl_gm1_short, log10(tau_fit_gm1_short));

tau_fit_gm1_long = tau_y(idx_gm1_long);
fit_gm1_long = 10.^predict(mdl_gm1_long, log10(tau_fit_gm1_long));

% AR(1) theoretical Allan deviation
phi = F;
sigma2 = std_y^2;

n = m(:);
tau_avg = n * Ts;

var_mean = zeros(size(n));

for ii = 1:numel(n)
    h = (1:n(ii)-1)';
    var_mean(ii) = sigma2/n(ii)^2 * ...
        (n(ii) + 2*sum((n(ii)-h).*phi.^h));
end

cov_adj = sigma2 ./ n.^2 .* ...
    phi .* (1 - phi.^n).^2 ./ (1 - phi)^2;

avar_theory = var_mean - cov_adj;
adev_theory = sqrt(avar_theory);

% ************
% Final figure
% ************

figure

h_fit_white = loglog(tau_fit_white, fit_white, ...
    'r', 'LineWidth', 2);
hold on

h_theory = loglog(tau_avg, adev_theory, ...
    'k', 'LineWidth', 1);

h_fit_gm1_short = loglog(tau_fit_gm1_short, fit_gm1_short, ...
    'r', 'LineWidth', 2);

loglog(tau_fit_gm1_long, fit_gm1_long, ...
    'r', 'LineWidth', 2);

h_white = loglog(tau_u, adev_u, ...
    'k.', 'MarkerSize', 24);

h_gm1 = loglog(tau_y, adev_y, ...
    'b.', 'MarkerSize', 24);

grid on
ax = gca;
ax.XMinorGrid = 'off';
ax.YMinorGrid = 'off';
ax.GridAlpha = 0.15;

xlabel('Averaging time \tau [s]')
ylabel('Allan deviation')

legend([h_white, h_gm1, h_fit_white, h_theory], ...
       {'white input', ...
        'GM1 output', ...
        'log-log fits', ...
        'AR(1) theory'}, ...
       'Location', 'southwest')

set(gca, 'FontSize', 14, 'LineWidth', 1.5)
```
:::



The Allan-deviation curves obtained from the simulated sequences are shown in @fig-allan.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Allan-deviation comparison between white noise and a GM1 process with correlation time $\tau_c = 1\,\mathrm{s}$. Red segments indicate local log--log regressions used for slope estimation, while the solid black curve represents the theoretical AR(1) prediction.](allan.png){#fig-allan fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::



Several important features immediately emerge from the comparison.

For the white-noise input, the Allan deviation follows the familiar power law

$$
\sigma_A(\tau) \propto \tau^{-1/2},
$$

indicating that longer averaging times continuously increase the amount of statistically independent information available through averaging. The corresponding log--log regression yields a slope of $-0.500$ ($95\%$ CI $[-0.502,-0.497]$), in excellent agreement with the theoretical value $-1/2$.

The GM1 process behaves very differently. At very short averaging times, its Allan deviation initially lies below the white-noise reference because the first-order dynamics suppress rapid fluctuations and smooth the process locally. However, as the averaging time approaches the correlation-time region, the effects of temporal memory progressively dominate the averaging process.

In this regime, consecutive observations no longer behave as statistically independent measurements. The Allan-deviation curve departs from the white-noise scaling law and exhibits a markedly different slope structure. The short-time log--log regression yields a positive slope of $0.371$ ($95\%$ CI $[0.296,0.446]$), directly reflecting the fact that local oversampling is collecting strongly correlated information rather than statistically independent samples.

Only for averaging times significantly longer than the correlation time does the process progressively recover a white-noise-like averaging behavior. In this asymptotic regime, the long-time slope approaches the classical $-1/2$ value expected for effectively decorrelated observations. The corresponding regression yields a slope of $-0.489$ ($95\%$ CI $[-0.582,-0.395]$).

The theoretical Allan-deviation curve derived from the equivalent AR(1) representation closely matches the simulated GM1 behavior across all averaging scales, further confirming the exact equivalence between the sampled Gauss--Markov process and its discrete-time autoregressive representation.

::: callout-note
## A closer look at Allan averaging

The Allan variance can be interpreted in a particularly illuminating way when the underlying process possesses temporal correlation.

For a sequence divided into adjacent blocks of length $n$, define the local averages

$$
\bar x_{1,n}=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n x_k,
$$

and

$$
\bar x_{2,n}=\frac1n\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n} x_k.
$$

The Allan variance is constructed from the squared difference between consecutive local averages:

$$
\sigma_A^2(n)=\frac12\mathbb E\left[(\bar X_{2,n}-\bar X_{1,n})^2\right].
$$

Using the elementary identity

$$
\mathrm{Var}(A-B)=\mathrm{Var}(A)+\mathrm{Var}(B)-2\mathrm{Cov}(A,B),
$$

and exploiting stationarity,

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_{1,n})=\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_{2,n}),
$$

one immediately obtains

$$
\sigma_A^2(n)=
\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_n)-\mathrm{Cov}(\bar X_{1,n},\bar X_{2,n}).
$$

This expression provides a remarkably intuitive interpretation of Allan variance.

The first term,

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_n),
$$

describes the uncertainty reduction produced by averaging. The second term,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\bar X_{1,n},\bar X_{2,n}),
$$

measures the temporal redundancy that survives between adjacent local averages.

For white noise, adjacent averages are statistically independent and the covariance term vanishes. Allan averaging therefore behaves exactly as expected from the familiar $1/\sqrt{n}$ law. For correlated processes such as GM1 or AR(1), however, adjacent averages remain statistically dependent over time scales comparable with the correlation time. The covariance term then becomes significant and partially compensates the statistical benefit of averaging.

In this sense, Allan deviation can be viewed as a multiscale diagnostic tool that measures not only how much averaging reduces uncertainty, but also how much temporal memory survives across successive averaging windows.
:::

## Concluding remarks

Starting from the elementary problem of estimating a constant from noisy observations, this short series progressively reconstructed some of the core ideas underlying Kalman filtering and stochastic signal modeling.

The sample mean first reappeared as a special limiting case of the Kalman filter with zero process noise. Introducing a finite process covariance $Q$ then transformed the estimator into a dynamic filter capable of continuously balancing memory, responsiveness, and uncertainty. Extending the discussion to first-order Gauss--Markov processes revealed how finite correlation times fundamentally modify the statistical meaning of averaging and oversampling.

The key lesson is that temporal correlation matters. Two stochastic processes may possess the same variance while carrying profoundly different amounts of independent information across time. Allan deviation makes this distinction immediately visible by exposing how variability evolves across averaging scales.

Throughout this post, temporal correlation was entirely attributed to the physical quantity being measured, while the sensor itself was treated as an ideal memoryless device corrupted only by white measurement noise. Real sensors, however, often possess internal dynamics, drift, and correlated noise of their own.

In the final post of this series, we will move this temporal memory directly into the measurement process itself. Using state augmentation techniques, we will see how Kalman filters can be extended to estimate not only the physical state, but also the hidden dynamics of the sensor noise corrupting the observations.
